reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused either by a recurrent 17q21.31 microdeletion or by an intragenic variant in KANSL1, the single critical gene at the locus
Affected individuals are often noted to have a friendly, sociable, and amiable disposition
Neonatal and childhood hypotonia with developmental delay and intellectual disability is characteristic
Epilepsy occurs in a substantial proportion and should be actively sought and treated
Ptosis and distinctive facial features, including a long face and tubular or pear-shaped nose, are common
The recurrent deletion is associated with a specific parental chromosome 17 inversion polymorphism that predisposes to the rearrangement
Because KANSL1 is the causative gene, an intragenic sequence variant produces the same phenotype as the whole-gene deletion
Diagnosis is by chromosomal microarray for the deletion or by sequencing of KANSL1
reference.pathophysiology: Koolen-de Vries syndrome results from reduced dosage of KANSL1 on chromosome 17q21.31, whether through a recurrent microdeletion of the surrounding region or a loss-of-function variant within the gene itself. KANSL1 encodes a component of a histone acetyltransferase complex that modifies chromatin and thereby regulates the expression of many downstream genes during development. Haploinsufficiency disturbs this epigenetic regulation, affecting neuronal development and function and producing the intellectual disability, hypotonia, epilepsy, and characteristic facial features. The recurrent deletion is facilitated by a common inversion polymorphism of the region carried by a parent, which places the chromosome at increased risk of the non-allelic homologous recombination that generates the deletion.
additionalDifferentials: Other microdeletion syndromes presenting with hypotonia and intellectual disability
Other chromatin-modifier disorders such as Kabuki syndrome
Congenital myopathies and other causes of early hypotonia
Genetic epilepsy syndromes with developmental delay
Ptosis-associated syndromes such as blepharophimosis syndrome
Non-specific syndromic intellectual disability identified on broad genetic testing
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to detect the recurrent 17q21.31 deletion
Sequencing of KANSL1 when microarray is normal but the phenotype fits
Electroencephalography and neurological assessment for suspected seizures
Ophthalmological review for ptosis and associated eye findings
Developmental and cognitive assessment to guide support
Parental studies including assessment for the predisposing inversion polymorphism
redFlags: New or poorly controlled seizures requiring prompt neurological management
Ptosis obstructing the visual axis and threatening amblyopia
Significant feeding difficulty or aspiration related to hypotonia
Congenital anomalies such as cardiac or renal defects needing evaluation
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is generally not shortened, and the outlook is defined by lifelong intellectual disability of variable degree together with the sociable temperament that is typical of the condition; epilepsy is often manageable, and most individuals make developmental progress with appropriate educational and therapeutic support, though independent living is usually limited.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal microarray excludes the diagnosis when a KANSL1 sequence variant can produce the same condition
Overlooking epilepsy because the child's amiable behaviour masks concern
Missing ptosis severe enough to threaten vision in a young child
Failing to test a parent for the predisposing inversion when counselling on recurrence
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Early developmental intervention with physiotherapy for hypotonia and speech and language and occupational therapy, as there is no disease-specific therapy
Antiseizure medication with EEG-guided management of epilepsy, which affects a substantial proportion
Individualised educational and behavioural support that draws on the characteristically sociable temperament
Ophthalmological assessment and correction of ptosis and associated eye findings
Surveillance and management of associated congenital heart, renal and feeding problems
Genetic counselling with parental testing, including for the predisposing 17q21.31 inversion polymorphism
